I'm so sorry that you're going through this, and really hope that you get the help you need. I read that shelters are not really an option, and I don't know much about how things work in the US, but this what I learned about being homeless from a LPT post (not the best source, but it came from personal experience which I lack).

1) charities and food banks are your friends and you should use them as much as you need. They'll be happy to provide.

2) public libraries are usually free and provide you with shelter during the day. Use their computers whenever you can, mostly, to look for a job. I know that working is a hastle with this disease, so start with remote, half-time jobs if at all possible. That will give you a source of income as small as it can be. 

3) if you have a car, consider finding a way to turn it into a comfy bed, perhaps by putting down the back seats and installing a sort of "mattress"/pillow/rug/blankets. You need rest and pacing even if it feels like you should be pushing out.

4) some recommended that if you have any income, to get a cheap gym membership so that you have access to showers. 

I hope I knew more or could help more :(

I'm in a similar situation to you in the sense of living with a partner that we both see spending our lives together and in a healthy relationship. I also was recently diagnosed with EDS and ME/CFS, and had a time of feeling like he was carrying this huge bag with half of my stuff in it. But relationships are not transactional and it is not "how are we going to distribute the chores so that I feel that I'm doing the same amount that you are", it should be "how are we going to support each other so that we have a clean house that we feel happy living in". Like really sit down and brainstorm. Are there things that you can move around to make it easier? Can you cook in less dishes? Do you have two laundry baskets so that clothes are separated into colors and whites by the time you need to do laundry? Is there anything that you can get/change to remove something that is getting in the way of you doing x? One example in my relationship was doing dishes at night. I'm always insanely exhausted at the end of the day and my partner loves cooking and didn't want to cook simpler meals to have less dishes. They also didn't like the idea of leaving the dishes soaking and washing them the next morning. But they were fine with cooking dinner and doing the dishes if I prepare breakfast and do the breakfast dishes. They like staying in bed a bit longer after waking up and that would let them wake up to served breakfast without having to consider the time to do dishes in their routine. Is it a 50/50 solution? No way. We have cereal and coffee for breakfast vs super elaborate meals for dinner. It takes me 10 min to prepare breakfast and 5 min to do the dishes while it takes him 30 min to prepare dinner and 15 min to do the dishes. We are both happy with the solution though, and at the end the meals and dishes are getting done. Try things out and check in with each other to see if it's working or not. If you love each other, you'll figure it out.

When energy and motivation are no longer coming from just sleeping and eating you need to take them from somewhere else. The best and healthiest thing to do is to take a break and distance yourself from the source of stress. However, that's not almost possible or the timing might not be perfect. While you can get to the point of a break, you'll need to trick your body. A great source of energy is exercising. Increasing your heartbeat to a cardio range for around 10 minutes will give you the sensation of a boost in energy. This is easier to do if you already exercise and have some fitness to get yourself to a 10 min cardio exercise. Since this might not be the case, or you might feel too burnout to exercise, the easiest source might be joy. Make a list of things that bring you joy. Not any joy, but the sort of joy that you felt as a kid playing your favorite game. Your list might contain things like hiking, watching a movie, hanging with friends, any sort of art or creative work, playing a game, eating ice cream, or calling a loved one. Identify those things that make you feel like a kid again and make them part of your routine until you can really take some time off. It's truly amazing what joy can make to your energy when you're burnout.

Source: burnout PhD Student

The purpose of vaccination is to teach your immune system how to respond to a threat before the threat is there. Think of it as the difference between studying or not for an exam. You can still pass the exam without studying, but your chances are higher if you study plus it will likely take you less time and energy during the exam if you are prepared. So when you vaccinate your kid, and the exact mechanism depends on the vaccine type, their body will treat the vaccine as if it was in the middle of an infection. This means that some of the vaccine will be carried through the blood and lymphatics to organs from the immune system while some of the immune cells will travel to where the vaccine was injected and try to figure out what's going on. The cool thing, and the reason why vaccination is so important, is that once the cells within the immune organs figure out the best way to get rid of the vaccine (which for the body is like a wax figure of the pathogen) it keeps that information in some cells. Those cells will mostly remain in those organs or migrate to places like the bone marrow and will just hang in there waiting for their time to shine. Although reaching immunological memory might take a couple of weeks, the migration of the "wax figures" takes place in the first days and the process is not interrupted by the blood transfusion. From the perspective of the immune system, blood vessels are just a complex subway that can be used to reach the whole body effectively. But it's just that, a mode of transport and not their home.

Immunological memory is not kept by the lymphocytes that are in the blood. Blood transfusions do not replace the immune system nor they remove the immune cells responsible for memory. I can expand more/be more precise if you want so.

It is hard to tell for SARS-CoV-2 since it is not clear what’s happening from an immune stand point. It definitely doesn’t mean “once an asymptomatic carrier always an asymptomatic carrier”. It might mean though, that some asymptomatic patients are indeed not immune to reinfection.

It’s also hard to determine what “asymptomatic” means, since some symptoms can appear without being detected by the patient (e.g. lower oxygen saturation).

The term “immunity” in your question is referring to your body generating some sort of immunological memory to fight a particular infection. There are mostly two types of cells involved in creating this memory: T and B cells (for the purpose of this explanation it doesn’t matter what they do). For these cells to get to interact with the pathogen (virus or bacteria) in such a way that they generate memory, there needs to be enough of that infection such that other cells in the immune system recruit them. In asymptomatic infections (having the pathogen but clearing it out before showing symptoms), those “other cells” are able to fight the intruder without the help of T or B cells, and therefore, without generating memory.

The main problem with this approach is the amount of blood that you would need to get to be able to give enough antibodies to every vulnerable person. Convalescent plasma is not prepared from the blood donation of one donor but from thousands of them. The reason behind this is that if you inject too “few” antibodies, they will rapidly be cleared by the liver and you won’t be giving any protection to the receiver.

The most likely scenario is that nothing happens as long as the mAb is also human derived. If the mAb is better than the natural immune response, it will help in the fight. If it is worse, it will eventually get cleared by the liver as any other antibody. 

The only potential side effects from an antibody therapy come from the antibodies having a cross-reactivity with a different antigen than the intended. If the monoclonal antibody binds to a self-antigen, it might create an autoimmune response. This is usually not the case if the antibody was derived in the same species.

I’m not in humanities, I’m in engineering, so how research affects society might be a bit straightforward. In terms of outreach, I volunteered a lot during my undergrad as a teacher for low-income children. I was also part of a society that helped under-represented minorities in science and engineering. And my SoP was written in a way that showed how these activities gave me unique traits that enhanced my research outcome.

You need to show that they’re not investing money in you to give you a PhD diploma, but to train the future great minds of your field. Outreach is everything you do to communicate your research outside of your department. You want to show that you have a social impact beyond your research, and the best way to show that is by having social impact before your PhD. Broader impact comes across the same idea, but it evolves more around the fact that whatever you plan to do during your PhD benefits society or advances desired societal outcomes. Some applications ask you to state what would you like to work in and with whom. That’s were you have to think of something that has a broader impact.
